extracted.intended_audience: research funders, meta-researchers, evaluation teams, and policy makers interested in grant allocation processes
extracted.subtask_description: Reviewing and recommending metrics, measurement approaches and evaluation frameworks to assess bias, burden and conservatism (including support for innovation) across research grant funding processes. Applicable to funders seeking to analyse and improve their application/review/award systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Level of burden
rubrics_metrics.description: Level of burden (as a primary objective of the study) — burden on researchers, institutions and funding bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure burden across stakeholders and across stages (application, review, reporting, project conduct). Use indicators such as time to prepare an application, number of pages/sections, administrative costs, frequency of reporting, application time per applicant, and downstream time/effort for institutions and funders. Consider both absolute burden and relative burden (e.g. by career stage or institution size). The paper emphasises that burden can emerge at many wider stages in the development and implementation of a funding scheme, not only at the application/review phase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of bias in funding processes — the paper frames bias as a core challenge funders should measure and addresses multiple potential sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether processes are fair and objective; identify systematic patterns disadvantaging particular applicant groups. Use comparable quantitative studies where possible, acknowledging heterogeneity across programmes. Combine historical funding data analysis with complementary methods (see measurement approaches entry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant characteristics (collect & analyse)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant characteristics collected during grant application processes may include gender, age, race, ethnicity and nationality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure applications capture relevant demographic and career variables (where lawful and ethical). Analyse outcomes by these characteristics; be cautious about visibility/observability of some attributes (e.g. ethnicity may be inferred from names/affiliation). Disaggregate outcomes at multiple stages (application, pre-selection, interview, award).

rubrics_metrics.name: Gender bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Gender bias (highlighted as the primary area of study within applicant characteristics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use statistical analyses to compare success rates and score distributions by gender, examine differences in reviewer language (text mining of critiques), and investigate whether gender interacts with other predictors (e.g. h-index, prior funding). Compare effects on 'quality of researcher' vs 'quality of proposal' scores. Consider longitudinal approaches and meta-analyses; note mixed evidence across contexts (some funders find bias, others do not).

rubrics_metrics.name: Racial / ethnic bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Racial/ethnic bias in grant peer review and award outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse funding rates controlling for background variables (education, training, prior awards, publication record, employer). Experimental approaches (e.g., name-modification experiments) can detect bias at the review stage. Interpret cautiously — bias may appear at other stages beyond review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Career stage bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Bias relating to career stage (including issues with defining career stage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider multiple operationalisations (career age since highest degree, functional competence-based stages such as the European Framework for Research Careers). Analyse trends that may disadvantage early-career researchers (e.g., rising average age of grantees). Adjust for career breaks, clinical or teaching commitments where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research field and interdisciplinarity bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Bias between research fields and against interdisciplinary research; interdisciplinarity may reduce funding probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop or use metrics to capture interdisciplinarity (the paper cites the interdisciplinary distance (IDD) metric). Test whether degree of interdisciplinarity predicts lower success rates; control for field-specific norms. Beware definitional challenges in identifying interdisciplinary proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Bias related to applicant institution characteristics (e.g., institution size, prestige).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse success and quantity of funding by institution size and type. Distinguish between bias due to true differences in merit/research environment and bias due to preferential treatment. Consider forecasting models and regression approaches to isolate institutional effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer characteristics and reviewer-related bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer characteristics (expertise, nationality, social environment, prior citation ties) can affect evaluations and introduce bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure reviewer expertise proximity (e.g., citation overlap) and test its association with funding. Examine reviewer nationality and social environment effects. Monitor reviewer assignment procedures to avoid systematic advantages; consider reviewer training and selection policies to improve fairness. Report reviewer-level variance and patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robustness of peer review: fairness, objectivity, reliability, validity and generalisability
rubrics_metrics.description: A robust peer review process must be fair and objective; evaluation should consider reliability, validity, bias, and generalisability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use inter-rater reliability statistics, validation studies (predictive validity of scores for later outcomes), and assessments of generalisability across programmes. Where possible, benchmark across funders and use external program evaluation to verify conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Summary of measurement approaches used to study bias: Statistical evaluation of funding data; Bibliometrics; Text mining and analysis; Longitudinal studies; Experimental randomisation; New metrics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select one or more complementary methods depending on data availability and question. Examples: multilevel regression on funding datasets, bibliometric proxies for career stage or productivity, text mining of reviewer critiques to detect linguistic bias, longitudinal follow-up for career impacts, randomized experiments (e.g., anonymity/name manipulation) to isolate causal bias, and development of bespoke metrics (e.g., IDD for interdisciplinarity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Metrics and indicators (bibliometric and administrative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Metrics and indicators used include h-index, prior funding, publication/citation measures, and administrative indicators captured by funders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use bibliometrics cautiously as proxies for merit; understand field differences and gaming risks. Combine bibliometric indicators with application- and reviewer-level data. Track which metrics are used in decision-making and test their predictive and fairness properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supporting innovation and creativity (measuring innovation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures and approaches to assess whether funding supports innovative and creative research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalise innovation (e.g., novelty, interdisciplinarity, high-risk/high-reward outputs) and track downstream outcomes (publications, citations, patents, societal impact) longitudinally. Consider funder policies that aim to encourage innovation (wildcards, investigator-driven funding proportions, continuous funding rounds) and evaluate their effects on diversity and novelty of funded research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservatism in funding decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Tendency of funding processes to favour conservative, incremental research or established investigators over novel approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure conservatism via associations between prior outputs/prior funding and success, lower funding probability for interdisciplinary or novel projects, and reviewer language indicating risk aversion. Design interventions to enable risky/novel proposals (e.g., separate streams, wildcards) and evaluate their uptake and outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application process features affecting bias and burden
rubrics_metrics.description: Application design elements (length of application, short vs long forms, ROPE statements, pre-screening/triage, continuous funding rounds, mid-point/end-point reviews) affect burden and possibly bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure how changes to application format (e.g., shortened forms) affect applicant time, success rates, and applicant mix. Evaluate pre-screening for burden reduction (e.g., CV-based triage) and consider unintended consequences (e.g., cherry-picking applicants). Use experimental or quasi-experimental evaluation where possible to infer effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and openness (data sharing and external evaluation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Transparency of funders (e.g., opening anonymised application data for scrutiny, external programme evaluation) as a criterion to assess and improve funding processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage publication of anonymised datasets, evaluation reports and external programme evaluations. Use transparency to enable independent reanalysis and benchmarking; balance openness with privacy/ethical constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation framework and data extraction template items
rubrics_metrics.description: Data extraction template headers used for evaluating literature and practice: objectives, area of peer review, evaluation framework/model, evidence on measures of burden/bias/innovation, datasets and collection, metrics and indicators, challenges, strengths/weaknesses, quality of study design and conduct, strength and generalisability of findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When conducting evaluations or evidence reviews, extract consistent headers and rate study quality and generalisability (the authors used red/amber/green). Use a pre-specified coding framework aligned to study aims to ensure systematic extraction and comparability across studies/organisations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality and generalisability ratings for evaluation studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign assessments such as 'Quality of study design and conduct (red, amber, green)' and 'Strength and generalisability of the findings (assign red, amber, or green)'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply transparent criteria for rating internal validity and external generalisability of evaluation studies. Use these ratings to weight evidence when synthesising findings and recommending policy changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of experimental designs to detect bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental randomisation (e.g., name manipulation experiments) to test causal effects of applicant characteristics on review outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When feasible, implement randomized or quasi-experimental designs to isolate causal bias at the review stage (e.g., swapping names/identifiers, anonymised review trials). Interpret results alongside observational analyses, as experiments may capture only some stages of the funding process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer workload and panel processes (number of reviewers, inter-rater agreement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Operational reviewer variables such as number of reviewers per application, inter-rater reliability, and training to improve consistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure and report inter-rater agreement statistics and analyze how panel composition and reviewer numbers affect outcomes. Consider reviewer training interventions to improve reliability (evidence cited that training can improve inter-rater reliability). Evaluate trade-offs between thorough review (more reviewers) and burden on reviewers and applicants.
